title: 2b — Programs That Make Choices

content.title: What If Your Program Could Decide?
content.summary: if lets your program check something and only run certain code when it's true.
content.body: Right now your programs run every line, top to bottom, no matter what. But what if you wanted a program that did something different depending on the player's answer? That's where if comes in. if lets your program check something — and only do something when that check is true.

content.title: Writing an if Statement
content.summary: Write if, then a condition, then a colon. The indented lines below only run if the condition is true.
content.body:
Here's the shape of an if statement:

if something == "value":
    print("It matched!")

The == means "is equal to" — two equals signs, not one.
The indented line only runs if the check is true.
If it's false, Python skips it and moves on.

content.title: Indentation Matters — A Lot
content.summary: The code inside an if MUST be indented (4 spaces or a Tab). Python uses indentation to know what belongs inside the if.
content.body:
Python uses spaces (or a Tab) to know which lines belong inside the if. If a line is indented — pushed in by 4 spaces — it's "inside" the if. If it's back at the edge, it's outside.

This is one of the most common places to get an error. If you see an IndentationError, check whether the lines inside your if are pushed in!

content.title: Try It: A Favourite Colour Checker
content.summary: Ask for a favourite colour. If it matches, print a special message.
content.body:
favorite = input("Favorite color? ")

if favorite == "blue":
    print("Blue is awesome!")

Run it and type "blue" — you should see the message. Now try typing something else. What happens? The program just stays silent because the check wasn't true.
